issues.explanation: 'People cycling' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile for a refugee trauma presentation when the other triggers are funerals/graves and car sounds, and there are no corresponding memory or appraisal items suggesting bicycles or a cycling-related trauma cue. This trigger looks clinically disconnected from the stated trauma context and the rest of the network.

'I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. In an older married male refugee with severe PTSD symptoms, self-harm can occur, but here it is the only extreme behavioral regulation item and is unsupported by the other selected strategies, memories, or appraisals. It appears clinically out of pattern relative to the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation.

vignette: Mr. Rajiv Patel, a 75-year-old South Asian man, is seeking help after decades of struggling with the aftermath of his traumatic past as a refugee. Born and raised in India, Mr. Patel moved to America several years ago following the harrowing experiences that marked his journey from conflict. The most vivid recollection he has is of a funeral procession for fellow refugees who did not survive the escape from their war-torn homeland. The sight of graves and mourners, the sounds of cars passing by—a recurring auditory trigger—and even the presence of authority figures like police officers all evoke intense feelings that transport him back to those terrifying moments. Mr. Patel has come to believe he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him as a potter; this sense of diminished capability stems from these potent triggers. The constant reminders of his past trauma leave him feeling overwhelmed and unable to cope with even minor upsets, which reinforces his belief in his inability to function as he once did. His memories of those traumatic events are more real than ordinary recollections, often appearing as disconnected fragments that do not fit together seamlessly. This nonverbal memory, vivid yet disjointed, has led him to avoid situations that might trigger these distressing thoughts. For instance, he avoids any gatherings or positive events because they remind him too acutely of the loss and grief associated with his past. Mr. Patel’s preoccupation with constant vigilance—constantly scanning his environment for signs of threat—has become a maladaptive strategy that further entrenches his negative appraisals. He frequently checks surroundings, which often leads to heightened anxiety and reinforces his belief in the necessity of such vigilance. This pattern has resulted in him avoiding any potential conflicts or disagreements at work, believing these could escalate into more dangerous situations. The fragmented memories also fuel his avoidance behaviors. The inability to articulate what he experienced clearly means that he remains trapped within those disjointed images and sensations, unable to fully process them. Consequently, his coping mechanisms have become increasingly rigid and isolating. He has distanced himself from friends and family, fearing that any positive emotions could be overshadowed by the memories of his past. The culmination of these experiences has led Mr. Patel to a state where he feels perpetually on edge. His marriage has been strained as he struggles to engage in activities with his wife without being haunted by the triggers that are omnipresent in his daily life. The weight of his trauma has made it difficult for him to continue working, and he often finds himself unable to focus on crafting pottery, a skill that once brought him immense joy. What finally prompted Mr. Patel to seek help was an incident where he avoided attending a local community event celebrating the heritage of refugees. He realized then that his avoidance had become so extreme that it was interfering with his ability to connect with others who shared similar experiences. Despite his fears, Mr. Patel is hopeful that therapy can provide him with tools to manage these overwhelming memories and triggers, allowing him to reclaim aspects of his life that have been lost to the shadows of trauma. In this journey toward healing, Mr. Patel hopes to regain a sense of normalcy and reconnect with the joy he once found in his craft and relationships.
